claim: PPP-family phosphatases such as PP1 have little intrinsic specificity.
source: PPP-family phosphatases such as PP1 have little intrinsic specificity.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about PP1 phosphatases.

claim: Cofactors can target PP1 to substrates or subcellular locations.
source: Cofactors can target PP1 to substrates or subcellular locations, but it remains unclear how they might confer sequence-specificity on PP1.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is referenced in the introduction.

claim: Phactr1 is a neuronally enriched PP1 cofactor that is controlled by G-actin.
source: The cytoskeletal regulator Phactr1 is a neuronally enriched PP1 cofactor that is controlled by G-actin.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work in the introduction section.

claim: Phactr1 binding remodels PP1's hydrophobic groove, creating a new composite surface adjacent to the catalytic site.
source: Structural analysis showed that Phactr1 binding remodels PP1's hydrophobic groove, creating a new composite surface adjacent to the catalytic site.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data presented in the manuscript, specifically the crystal structures.

claim: Phactr1/PP1 substrates include cytoskeletal components and regulators.
source: Using phosphoproteomics, we identified mouse fibroblast and neuronal Phactr1/PP1 substrates, which include cytoskeletal components and regulators.
evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: High-resolution structures of Phactr1/PP1 bound to dephosphorylated forms of IRSp53 and spectrin αII were determined.
source: We determined high-resolution structures of Phactr1/PP1 bound to the dephosphorylated forms of its substrates IRSp53 and spectrin αII.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inversion of the phosphate in holoenzyme-product complexes supports the proposed PPP-family catalytic mechanism.
source: Inversion of the phosphate in these holoenzyme-product complexes supports the proposed PPP-family catalytic mechanism.
evidence: This is based on structural observations and inference from the crystal structures.

claim: Substrate sequences C-terminal to the dephosphorylation site make intimate contacts with the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface.
source: Substrate sequences C-terminal to the dephosphorylation site make intimate contacts with the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface, which are required for efficient dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Phactr1/PP1 exhibits orders-of-magnitude enhanced reactivity towards its substrates compared to apo-PP1 or other PP1 holoenzymes.
source: Sequence specificity explains why Phactr1/PP1 exhibits orders-of-magnitude enhanced reactivity towards its substrates, compared to apo-PP1 or other PP1 holoenzymes.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data comparing different PP1 complexes.

claim: PPP family phosphatases carry out the majority of protein serine/threonine dephosphorylation.
source: PPP family phosphatases are metalloenzymes that carry out the majority of protein serine/threonine dephosphorylation (Brautigan and Shenolikar, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brautigan and Shenolikar, 2018.

claim: PP1 has three isoforms that regulate diverse cellular processes.
source: The three Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) isoforms regulate diverse cellular processes, acting in partnership with over 200 different PP1-interacting proteins (PIPs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bollen et al., 2010 and Cohen, 2002.

claim: PP1 acts in partnership with over 200 different PP1-interacting proteins (PIPs).
source: The three Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) isoforms regulate diverse cellular processes, acting in partnership with over 200 different PP1-interacting proteins (PIPs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bollen et al., 2010 and Cohen, 2002.

claim: Some PIPs are PP1 substrates, while others are PP1 cofactors.
source: Some PIPs are PP1 substrates, but others are PP1 cofactors, which variously determine substrate specificity, subcellular targeting and/or coupling to regulatory pathways (Bollen et al., 2010; Cohen, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bollen et al., 2010 and Cohen, 2002.

claim: The PP1 catalytic site lies at the intersection of three putative substrate-binding grooves.
source: The PP1 catalytic site lies at the intersection of three putative substrate-binding grooves (Egloff et al., 1995; Goldberg et al., 1995), and PIPs can interact both with these grooves and with other PP1 surface features.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egloff et al., 1995 and Goldberg et al., 1995.

claim: PIPs can interact with PP1 substrate-binding grooves and other PP1 surface features.
source: The PP1 catalytic site lies at the intersection of three putative substrate-binding grooves (Egloff et al., 1995; Goldberg et al., 1995), and PIPs can interact both with these grooves and with other PP1 surface features.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: PIPs use a variety of short sequence elements to interact with PP1, of which the RVxF motif is the best understood.
source: To do this they use a variety of short sequence elements, of which the best understood is the RVxF motif (Choy et al., 2014; Egloff et al., 1997; Hendrickx et al., 2009; Hurley et al., 2007; O'Connell et al., 2012; Ragusa et al., 2010; Terrak et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: PP1 exhibits little sequence-specificity by itself.
source: Unlike protein Ser/Thr kinases, PP1 exhibits little sequence-specificity by itself (Brautigan and Shenolikar, 2018; Miller and Turk, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brautigan and Shenolikar, 2018 and Miller and Turk, 2018.

claim: No instances of PIP-induced sequence-specificity are known.
source: Moreover, no instances of PIP-induced sequence-specificity are known, although it is well established that PIPs can enhance or inhibit PP1 activity towards particular substrates (Ichikawa et al., 1996; Johnson et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: PIPs can enhance or inhibit PP1 activity towards particular substrates.
source: Moreover, no instances of PIP-induced sequence-specificity are known, although it is well established that PIPs can enhance or inhibit PP1 activity towards particular substrates (Ichikawa et al., 1996; Johnson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ichikawa et al., 1996 and Johnson et al., 1996.

claim: Some PIPs contain autonomous substrate-binding domains that facilitate substrate recruitment.
source: Some PIPs contain autonomous substrate-binding domains, which facilitate substrate recruitment (Boudrez et al., 2000; Choy et al., 2015), while others constrain substrate specificity by occluding PP1 surfaces such as the RVxF-binding pocket and/or substrate-binding grooves (Hirschi et al., 2010; Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boudrez et al., 2000 and Choy et al., 2015.

claim: Some PIPs constrain substrate specificity by occluding PP1 surfaces such as the RVxF-binding pocket and/or substrate-binding grooves.
source: Some PIPs contain autonomous substrate-binding domains, which facilitate substrate recruitment (Boudrez et al., 2000; Choy et al., 2015), while others constrain substrate specificity by occluding PP1 surfaces such as the RVxF-binding pocket and/or substrate-binding grooves (Hirschi et al., 2010; Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hirschi et al., 2010 and Ragusa et al., 2010.

claim: Several PIPs extend the PP1 substrate-binding grooves and/or significantly alter PP1 surface electrostatics without altering the conformation of the catalytic site.
source: Interestingly, several PIPs extend the PP1 substrate-binding grooves and/or significantly alter PP1 surface electrostatics, without altering the conformation of the catalytic site (O'Connell et al., 2012; Ragusa et al., 2010; Terrak et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Connell et al., 2012, Ragusa et al., 2010, and Terrak et al., 2004.

claim: The four Phosphatase and actin regulator (Phactr) proteins are novel PIPs implicated in cytoskeletal regulation.
source: The four Phosphatase and actin regulator (Phactr) proteins (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2003) are novel PIPs that are implicated in cytoskeletal regulation in animal models (Hamada et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012) and cell culture settings (Huet et al., 2013; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Phactrs bind G-actin via multiple RPEL motifs present in their conserved N- and C-terminal regions.
source: The Phactrs bind G-actin via multiple RPEL motifs present in their conserved N- and C-terminal regions (Huet et al., 2013; Mouilleron et al., 2012; Sagara et al., 2009; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huet et al., 2013, Mouilleron et al., 2012, Sagara et al., 2009, and Wiezlak et al., 2012.

claim: The Phactr C-terminal RPEL domain overlaps the PP1 binding sequence.
source: Their C-terminal RPEL domain overlaps the PP1 binding sequence (Allen et al., 2004; Larson et al., 2008; Sagara et al., 2003), and G-actin competes with PP1 for Phactr binding (Huet et al., 2013; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Allen et al., 2004, Larson et al., 2008, and Sagara et al., 2003.

claim: G-actin competes with PP1 for Phactr binding.
source: Their C-terminal RPEL domain overlaps the PP1 binding sequence (Allen et al., 2004; Larson et al., 2008; Sagara et al., 2003), and G-actin competes with PP1 for Phactr binding (Huet et al., 2013; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huet et al., 2013 and Wiezlak et al., 2012.

claim: G-actin/Phactr interactions respond to fluctuations in actin dynamics.
source: As a result, like other RPEL proteins, G-actin/Phactr interactions respond to fluctuations in actin dynamics (Diring et al., 2019; Miralles et al., 2003; Vartiainen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diring et al., 2019, Miralles et al., 2003, and Vartiainen et al., 2007.

claim: Extracellular signals control Phactr/PP1 complex formation through the rho-actin signal pathway by inducing changes in cellular G-actin concentration.
source: Extracellular signals, acting through the 'rho-actin' signal pathway, thus control Phactr/PP1 complex formation by inducing changes in cellular G-actin concentration (Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wiezlak et al., 2012.

claim: Phactr1 and Phactr3 inhibit dephosphorylation of phosphorylase a by PP1 in vitro.
source: Phactr1 and Phactr3 inhibit dephosphorylation of phosphorylase a by PP1 in vitro (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2003), but Phactr4/PP1 complex formation is associated with cofilin dephosphorylation in vivo (Huet et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Allen et al., 2004 and Sagara et al., 2003.

claim: Phactr4/PP1 complex formation is associated with cofilin dephosphorylation in vivo.
source: Phactr1 and Phactr3 inhibit dephosphorylation of phosphorylase a by PP1 in vitro (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2003), but Phactr4/PP1 complex formation is associated with cofilin dephosphorylation in vivo (Huet et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huet et al., 2013 and Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: Phactr1 confers sequence-specificity on the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme.
source: Here, we show that Phactr1 confers sequence-specificity on the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Efficient catalysis by Phactr1/PP1 requires interactions between conserved hydrophobic residues in the substrate and a novel Phactr1-PP1 composite surface.
source: We show that efficient catalysis requires interactions between conserved hydrophobic residues in the substrate and a novel Phactr1-PP1 composite surface, which comprises a hydrophobic pocket and associated amphipathic cavity with a surrounding basic rim.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Phactr1-PP1 composite surface comprises a hydrophobic pocket and associated amphipathic cavity with a surrounding basic rim.
source: We show that efficient catalysis requires interactions between conserved hydrophobic residues in the substrate and a novel Phactr1-PP1 composite surface, which comprises a hydrophobic pocket and associated amphipathic cavity with a surrounding basic rim.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from crystal structures.

claim: Phactr1/PP1 recognizes its substrates 100-fold more efficiently compared with PP1 alone or the spinophilin/PP1 complex.
source: These interactions allow Phactr1/PP1 to recognise its substrates 100-fold more efficiently compared with PP1 alone or the spinophilin/PP1 complex, in which the hydrophobic groove is remodelled differently.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data comparing different PP1 complexes.

claim: Phactr1 C-terminal sequences are necessary and sufficient for interaction with PP1.
source: Previous studies have shown that Phactr1 C-terminal sequences are necessary and sufficient for interaction with PP1 (Allen et al., 2004; Wiezlak et al., 2012): they contain an RVxF-like sequence, LIRF, and can functionally substitute for the related PP1-binding domain of yeast Bni4 (Larson et al., 2008; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Allen et al., 2004, Wiezlak et al., 2012, and Larson et al., 2008.

claim: Phactr1 contains an RVxF-like sequence, LIRF.
source: Previous studies have shown that Phactr1 C-terminal sequences are necessary and sufficient for interaction with PP1 (Allen et al., 2004; Wiezlak et al., 2012): they contain an RVxF-like sequence, LIRF, and can functionally substitute for the related PP1-binding domain of yeast Bni4 (Larson et al., 2008; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and citations.

claim: Phactr1(517-580) bound PP1α(7-300) with an affinity of 10.4 nM.
source: Phactr1(517-580) bound with an affinity of 10.4 nM, comparable to Phactr3, while the other Phactrs bound more weakly (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The Kd of Phactr1(517-580) for PP1 is similar to PIPs such as spinophilin (8.7 nM) and PNUTS (9.3 nM).
source: This Kd is similar to PIPs such as spinophilin (8.7 nM) and PNUTS (9.3 nM) (Choy et al., 2014; Ragusa et al., 2010), and somewhat stronger than PPP1R15A and NIPP1 (Choy et al., 2015; O'Connell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published data from Choy et al., 2014 and Ragusa et al., 2010.

claim: The structures of Phactr1(507-580)/PP1α(7-300) and Phactr1(516-580)/PP1α(7-300) were determined at 1.9 Å and 1.94 Å resolution, respectively.
source: We determined the structures of purified Phactr1(507-580)/PP1α(7-300) (1.9 Å) and Phactr1(516-580)/PP1α(7-300) (1.94 Å), which crystallised at pH 8.5 and pH 5.25, respectively, and exhibit differing conformations of Phactr1 residues C-terminal to residue 567 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: In both Phactr1/PP1 structures, the PP1 catalytic site contains two presumed manganese ions and a phosphate anion.
source: In both structures, the PP1 catalytic site contains two presumed manganese ions and a phosphate anion, as previously reported (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Egloff et al., 1995), and its conformation is virtually identical to that seen in other PP1 complexes, such as spinophilin/PP1 (RMSD 0.23 Å over 255 Cα atoms) (Choy et al., 2014; Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and comparison with previous structures.

claim: The PP1 conformation in Phactr1/PP1 is virtually identical to that seen in other PP1 complexes, such as spinophilin/PP1 (RMSD 0.23 Å over 255 Cα atoms).
source: In both structures, the PP1 catalytic site contains two presumed manganese ions and a phosphate anion, as previously reported (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Egloff et al., 1995), and its conformation is virtually identical to that seen in other PP1 complexes, such as spinophilin/PP1 (RMSD 0.23 Å over 255 Cα atoms) (Choy et al., 2014; Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with published structures.

claim: Phactr1 residues 516–542 wrap around PP1, occluding its C-terminal groove, and covering 2260 Å2 of solvent-accessible surface.
source: Phactr1 residues 516–542 wrap around PP1, occluding its C-terminal groove, and covering 2260 Å2 of solvent-accessible surface (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), contacting PP1 in a strikingly similar way to spinophilin, PNUTS and PPP1R15B (Chen et al., 2015; Choy et al., 2014; Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Phactr1 contacts PP1 in a strikingly similar way to spinophilin, PNUTS and PPP1R15B.
source: Phactr1 residues 516–542 wrap around PP1, occluding its C-terminal groove, and covering 2260 Å2 of solvent-accessible surface (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), contacting PP1 in a strikingly similar way to spinophilin, PNUTS and PPP1R15B (Chen et al., 2015; Choy et al., 2014; Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with published structures.

claim: The RVxF sequence LIRF(519-522) is critical for Phactr1/PP1 complex formation.
source: The RVxF sequence LIRF(519-522) is critical for Phactr1/PP1 complex formation (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). Its deletion decreased binding affinity ~104 fold, while the I520A and F522A mutations reduced it 4-fold and ~650 fold respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and binding affinity data.

claim: Deletion of the LIRF sequence decreased Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity ~104 fold.
source: Its deletion decreased binding affinity ~104 fold, while the I520A and F522A mutations reduced it 4-fold and ~650 fold respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The I520A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity 4-fold.
source: Its deletion decreased binding affinity ~104 fold, while the I520A and F522A mutations reduced it 4-fold and ~650 fold respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The F522A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity ~650 fold.
source: Its deletion decreased binding affinity ~104 fold, while the I520A and F522A mutations reduced it 4-fold and ~650 fold respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The RVxF residue L519 makes contacts with G-actin in the trivalent G-actin•Phactr1 RPEL domain complex.
source: The RVxF residue L519 also makes contacts with G-actin in the trivalent G-actin•Phactr1 RPEL domain complex (Mouilleron et al., 2012), explaining why PP1 and G-actin binding to Phactr proteins is mutually exclusive (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from Mouilleron et al., 2012.

claim: PP1 and G-actin binding to Phactr proteins is mutually exclusive.
source: The RVxF residue L519 also makes contacts with G-actin in the trivalent G-actin•Phactr1 RPEL domain complex (Mouilleron et al., 2012), explaining why PP1 and G-actin binding to Phactr proteins is mutually exclusive (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and citation to Wiezlak et al., 2012.

claim: Substitution of R536 by proline reduced Phactr1-binding affinity >300 fold.
source: Substitution of R536 by proline, as in the mouse Phactr4 'humdy' mutation (Kim et al., 2007), reduced Phactr1-binding affinity >300 fold, while Y534A reduced it > 10 fold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The Y534A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity > 10 fold.
source: Substitution of R536 by proline, as in the mouse Phactr4 'humdy' mutation (Kim et al., 2007), reduced Phactr1-binding affinity >300 fold, while Y534A reduced it > 10 fold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The W542A mutation reduced PP1-binding affinity ~40-fold.
source: Although W542A reduced PP1-binding affinity ~40-fold, R544A reduced it ~ threefold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The R544A mutation reduced PP1-binding affinity ~ threefold.
source: Although W542A reduced PP1-binding affinity ~40-fold, R544A reduced it ~ threefold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: Phactr1 residues 545–565 include a five-turn amphipathic α-helix that abuts the PP1 hydrophobic groove.
source: Residues 545–565 include a five-turn amphipathic α-helix that abuts the PP1 hydrophobic groove: Phactr1 residues L545, I553, L557, F560 make hydrophobic contacts with PP1 I133, R132, W149, and K150, while E556 and E564 make salt bridges with PP1 R132 and K150, respectively, and K561 hydrogen bonds with PP1 S129 and D194 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: A triple alanine substitution of Phactr1 L557, F560 and L574 (LFL-3A) resulted in a ~ 900 fold drop in binding affinity.
source: A triple alanine substitution of Phactr1 L557, F560 and L574 (LFL-3A) resulted in a ~ 900 fold drop in binding affinity, while the acidic substitution L574D reduced binding affinity by 17-fold.
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The L574D mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity by 17-fold.
source: A triple alanine substitution of Phactr1 L557, F560 and L574 (LFL-3A) resulted in a ~ 900 fold drop in binding affinity, while the acidic substitution L574D reduced binding affinity by 17-fold.
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The F577A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding activity by 16-fold.
source: Mutations F577A and H578A reduced binding activity by 16-fold and 7-fold, respectively, corroborating previous co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2009), and mutation of all three C-terminal histidines (HHH-A) reduced affinity >50 fold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The H578A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding activity by 7-fold.
source: Mutations F577A and H578A reduced binding activity by 16-fold and 7-fold, respectively, corroborating previous co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2009), and mutation of all three C-terminal histidines (HHH-A) reduced affinity >50 fold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: Mutation of all three C-terminal histidines (HHH-A) reduced Phactr1-PP1 affinity >50 fold.
source: Mutations F577A and H578A reduced binding activity by 16-fold and 7-fold, respectively, corroborating previous co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2009), and mutation of all three C-terminal histidines (HHH-A) reduced affinity >50 fold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claim: The docking of Phactr1 C-terminal sequences across the PP1 hydrophobic groove substantially modifies its topography.
source: The docking of Phactr1 C-terminal sequences across the PP1 hydrophobic groove substantially modifies its topography (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The positioning of the Phactr1 amphipathic helix creates a deep hydrophobic pocket comprising Phactr1 W542, L545, K550, I553, R554, L557 and H578, and PP1 I130 I133 and Y134.
source: The positioning of the Phactr1 amphipathic helix creates a deep hydrophobic pocket comprising Phactr1 W542, L545, K550, I553, R554, L557 and H578, and PP1 I130 I133 and Y134.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: A narrow amphipathic cavity is formed by the positioning of Phactr1 K561 and R576 across the PP1 hydrophobic groove.
source: Adjacent to the pocket, a narrow amphipathic cavity is formed by the positioning of Phactr1 K561 and R576 across the PP1 hydrophobic groove: its polar side comprises Phactr1 K561 and R576, and PP1 D194 and S129, while its hydrophobic side is formed from PP1 residues C127, I130, V195, W206 and V223.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Three water molecules and a glycerol are resolved within the amphipathic cavity.
source: Three water molecules and a glycerol are resolved within the cavity, whose hydrophobic side forms part of the binding site for the PP1 inhibitors tautomycetin and tautomycin (Choy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The hydrophobic side of the amphipathic cavity forms part of the binding site for the PP1 inhibitors tautomycetin and tautomycin.
source: Three water molecules and a glycerol are resolved within the cavity, whose hydrophobic side forms part of the binding site for the PP1 inhibitors tautomycetin and tautomycin (Choy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published structures from Choy et al., 2017.

claim: A basic rim is formed from Phactr1 residues K550, R554, R576, H578 and R579.
source: The new composite surface is crowned by a basic rim, formed from Phactr1 residues K550, R554, R576, H578 and R579 (Figure 2B), which radically alters the surface charge distribution (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Phactr1 binding radically alters the PP1 surface charge distribution.
source: The new composite surface is crowned by a basic rim, formed from Phactr1 residues K550, R554, R576, H578 and R579 (Figure 2B), which radically alters the surface charge distribution (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and electrostatic surface potential calculations.

claim: Phactr1 binding transforms the surface of PP1 adjacent to its catalytic site in a way distinct from that seen in the spinophilin/PP1 complex.
source: Thus, Phactr1 binding profoundly transforms the surface of PP1 adjacent to its catalytic site. This transformation is distinct from that seen in the spinophilin/PP1 complex (Ragusa et al., 2010), which modifies the hydrophobic groove in a different way and leaves the PP1 surface electrostatics unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with the spinophilin/PP1 complex.

claim: Expression of Phactr1XXX induces F-actin rearrangements in NIH3T3 fibroblasts, provided it can bind PP1.
source: We previously showed that expression of an activated Phactr1 derivative that constitutively forms the Phactr1/PP1 complex, Phactr1XXX, induces F-actin rearrangements in NIH3T3 fibroblasts, provided it can bind PP1 (Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wiezlak et al., 2012.

claim: Overexpression of the Phactr1 PP1-binding domain alone can induce cytoskeletal changes.
source: Indeed, overexpression of the Phactr1 PP1-binding domain alone can also induce such changes, suggesting that the Phactr1 C-terminal sequences are sufficient to allow recognition of at least some substrates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Over 3000 phosphorylation sites were quantified in the SILAC phosphoproteomics experiment.
source: Over 3000 phosphorylation sites were quantified, and each assigned a dephosphorylation score comparing their phosphorylation with that observed in cells inducibly expressing Phactr1XXXΔC, which lacks the PP1 binding sequences, or vector alone (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1, Table A).
evidence: This is supported by the SILAC phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Annotation enrichment analysis identified 'regulation of actin filament-based process' and 'regulation of actin cytoskeleton organisation' as categories with significantly higher mean dephosphorylation score upon expression of Phactr1XXX.
source: Annotation enrichment analysis of the whole dataset (Cox and Mann, 2012) identified two Gene Ontology Biological Process categories that exhibited a significantly higher mean dephosphorylation score upon expression of Phactr1XXX: 'regulation of actin filament-based process' and 'regulation of actin cytoskeleton organisation' (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1, Table B).
evidence: This is supported by annotation enrichment analysis of the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Proteins with a high dephosphorylation score included many cytoskeletal components and regulators.
source: In keeping with this, proteins with a high dephosphorylation score included many cytoskeletal components and regulators (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1, Table A).
evidence: This is supported by the SILAC phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Sites with dephosphorylation scores > 2.5 were enriched in acidic residues at positions +2 to +7 relative to the phosphorylation site, with small hydrophobic residues enriched at positions +4 and +5, and basic residues N-terminal to it.
source: Proline-directed sites predominated in the dataset as a whole, but those sites with dephosphorylation scores > 2.5 were enriched in acidic residues at positions +2 to +7 relative to the phosphorylation site, with small hydrophobic residues enriched at positions +4 and +5, and basic residues N-terminal to it (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis of the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: IRSp53 pS455 exhibited a low KM and high kcat/KM in the in vitro peptide dephosphorylation assay.
source: Synthetic phosphopeptides containing the candidate sites exhibited a range of KM and kcat/KM values: for example, IRSp53 pS455 exhibited a low KM and high kcat/KM; spectrin αII pS1031 had a similar KM but lower kcat/KM; and afadin pS1275 was as reactive as spectrin αII pS1031, but with much poorer KM (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claim: Spectrin αII pS1031 had a similar KM to IRSp53 pS455 but lower kcat/KM.
source: Synthetic phosphopeptides containing the candidate sites exhibited a range of KM and kcat/KM values: for example, IRSp53 pS455 exhibited a low KM and high kcat/KM; spectrin αII pS1031 had a similar KM but lower kcat/KM; and afadin pS1275 was as reactive as spectrin αII pS1031, but with much poorer KM (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claim: Afadin pS1275 was as reactive as spectrin αII pS1031, but with much poorer KM.
source: Synthetic phosphopeptides containing the candidate sites exhibited a range of KM and kcat/KM values: for example, IRSp53 pS455 exhibited a low KM and high kcat/KM; spectrin αII pS1031 had a similar KM but lower kcat/KM; and afadin pS1275 was as reactive as spectrin αII pS1031, but with much poorer KM (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claim: The four substrates with the lowest KM all contained a leucine doublet at the +4 and +5 positions.
source: Interestingly, the four substrates with the lowest KM - IRSp53 pS455, Plekho2 pS395, spectrin αII pS1031, and Tbc1d15 pS205 - all contained a leucine doublet at the +4 and +5 positions (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and kinetic data.

claim: Phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 was substantially decreased upon expression of Phactr1XXX in NIH3T3 cells.
source: Immunoblot analysis showed that in NIH3T3 cells, phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 was substantially decreased upon expression of Phactr1XXX, and by serum stimulation, which activates rho-actin signalling and Phactr-family/PP1 complex formation (Miralles et al., 2003; Vartiainen et al., 2007; Wiezlak et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claim: Serum stimulation decreased phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 in NIH3T3 cells.
source: Immunoblot analysis showed that in NIH3T3 cells, phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 was substantially decreased upon expression of Phactr1XXX, and by serum stimulation, which activates rho-actin signalling and Phactr-family/PP1 complex formation (Miralles et al., 2003; Vartiainen et al., 2007; Wiezlak et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claim: Treatment of NIH3T3 cells with cytochalasin D significantly decreased phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275.
source: Moreover, treatment of cells with cytochalasin D (CD), which binds G-actin and disrupts its interaction with RPEL proteins (Vartiainen et al., 2007; Wiezlak et al., 2012) significantly decreased phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claim: Treatment of NIH3T3 cells with latrunculin B increased phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275.
source: In contrast, treatment of cells with the latrunculin B (LB), which increases G-actin concentration through blockade of F-actin assembly, but whose binding to G-actin does not affect RPEL-actin interaction, had the opposite effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claim: Phactr1 mutations are associated with morphological and functional developmental defects in cortical neurons.
source: Phactr1 mutations are associated with morphological and functional developmental defects in cortical neurons (Hamada et al., 2018), and expression of Phactr1XXX induced morphological defects upon expression in cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamada et al., 2018.

claim: Expression of Phactr1XXX induced morphological defects in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Phactr1 mutations are associated with morphological and functional developmental defects in cortical neurons (Hamada et al., 2018), and expression of Phactr1XXX induced morphological defects upon expression in cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Phactr1-null mice are viable and do not show any obvious developmental abnormalities.
source: Phactr1-null mice are viable; they do not show any obvious developmental abnormalities, and expression of the other Phactr proteins is apparently unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by observations of the Phactr1-null mice.

claim: Expression of the other Phactr proteins is apparently unaffected in Phactr1-null mice.
source: Phactr1-null mice are viable; they do not show any obvious developmental abnormalities, and expression of the other Phactr proteins is apparently unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Among ~9000 phosphorylation sites quantified in the TMT phosphoproteomics experiment, 44 sites on 37 proteins differed significantly in their response to LB or CD stimuli in Phactr1-null cells.
source: Among ~9000 phosphorylation sites quantified, we found 44 sites on 37 proteins that differed significantly in their response to these stimuli in Phactr1-null cells (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 1, Table E).
evidence: This is supported by TMT phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Seven phosphorylation sites, including IRSp53 pS455, spectrin αII pS1031, and afadin pS1275, were observed in both NIH3T3 cells and neurons.
source: The sequence context of these sites was similar to that of those seen in NIH3T3 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), and seven, including IRSp53 pS455, spectrin αII pS1031, and afadin pS1275, were observed in both cell types (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of phosphoproteomics data from both cell types.

claim: The structures of the IRSp53(449-465) and spectrin αII (1025–1039) complexes were determined at 1.09 Å and 1.30 Å resolution, respectively.
source: This approach allowed determination of the structures of the IRSp53(449-465) and spectrin αII (1025–1039) complexes at 1.09 Å and 1.30 Å resolution, respectively (Figure 4A–C; Table 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; referred to hereafter as the IRSp53 and spectrin complexes), but was unsuccessful with Tbc1d15, Plekho2, afadin, and cofilin.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53 and Phactr1/PP1-spectrin complexes crystallised in the same spacegroup.
source: The Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53 and Phactr1/PP1-spectrin complexes crystallised in the same spacegroup.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: Each asymmetric unit of the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53 and Phactr1/PP1-spectrin complexes contains two complexes.
source: Each asymmetric unit contains two complexes (RMSD 0.22 Å and 0.17 Å over 288 Cα, respectively), in which substrate-Phactr1/PP1 interactions are mostly conserved, albeit with some minor differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The substrate sequences make extensive contacts across the PP1 catalytic site, then extend in a sinuous trajectory across the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface.
source: The substrate sequences, whose N-termini are largely unresolved, make extensive contacts across the PP1 catalytic site, then extend in a sinuous trajectory across the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface, making numerous hydrophobic and ionic contacts (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claim: The complexes contain a presumed phosphate anion at the catalytic site and appear to represent putative enzyme/product complexes.
source: Like the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme, the complexes contain a presumed phosphate anion at the catalytic site, and thus appear to represent putative enzyme/product complexes (see below).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and inference.

claim: The structure of Phactr1/PP1 in both substrate complexes is identical to that of the isolated Phactr1/PP1 complex.
source: The structure of Phactr1/PP1 in both complexes is identical to that of the isolated Phactr1/PP1 complex (RMSD 0.31 Å over 313 Cα and 0.32 Å over 307 Cα, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: IRSp53 and spectrin make virtually identical contacts with the PP1 catalytic cleft, predominantly via their mainchains.
source: IRSp53 and spectrin make virtually identical contacts with the PP1 catalytic cleft, predominantly via their mainchains (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claim: The phosphate is inverted in the substrate complexes compared with the holoenzyme complex.
source: The phosphate is inverted compared with the holoenzyme complex, losing its contact with PP1 R96 and H125, but making contact with the S455IRSp53/S1031spectrin hydroxyl (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The majority of the PP1 catalytic cleft residues that contact IRSp53 and spectrin are conserved among PPP family members, including PP5.
source: The majority of the PP1 catalytic cleft residues that contact IRSp53 and spectrin are conserved among PPP family members, including PP5, which has been crystallised in complex with a phosphomimetic derivative of its substrate, Cdc37(S13E) (Oberoi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by sequence conservation analysis and citation to Oberoi et al., 2016.

claim: In the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex, PP5 residues corresponding to PP1 R96, H125, Y134, R221, and Y272 make contacts with Cdc37(S13E) analogous to those seen in the Phactr1/PP1-substrate complexes, despite Cdc37(S13E) docking in the opposite orientation.
source: Strikingly, in that complex, the PP5 residues corresponding to PP1 R96, H125, Y134, R221, and Y272 make contacts with Cdc37(S13E) analogous to those seen in the Phactr1/PP1-substrate complexes, despite the fact that Cdc37(S13E) docks in the PP5 catalytic cleft in the opposite orientation to IRSp53 and spectrin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex.

claim: The phosphate in the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme structure is positioned similarly to the phosphorylated S455IRSp53/S1031spectrin of the bound substrate.
source: It is generally accepted that the phosphate seen in many PPP family protein structures binds the active site in a similar way to the substrate phosphate (Egloff et al., 1995; Griffith et al., 1995; Mueller et al., 1993; Swingle et al., 2004), and we therefore assume that the phosphate in our Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme structure is positioned similarly to the phosphorylated S455IRSp53/S1031spectrin of the bound substrate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and inference from the structures.

claim: In the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex, the phosphomimetic glutamate sidechain carbonyl is virtually superposable on the phosphate in the Phactr1/PP1 complex.
source: Consistent with this idea, in the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex, the phosphomimetic glutamate sidechain carbonyl is virtually superposable on the phosphate in the Phactr1/PP1 complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The Phactr1/PP1 complex contains a bound water, W1, presumably activated by the metal ions and PP1 D64 and D92.
source: The Phactr1/PP1 complex also contains a bound water, W1, presumably activated by the metal ions and PP1 D64 and D92 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and inference about the catalytic mechanism.

claim: W1 is oriented appropriately for in-line nucleophilic attack on the substrate phosphate.
source: W1 is oriented appropriately for in-line nucleophilic attack on the substrate phosphate: this would be facilitated by protonation of the phosphoserine oxygen by the PP1 catalytic dyad H125-D95, and would result in inversion of the phosphate (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and inference about the catalytic mechanism.

claim: The structures provide direct evidence for the in-line nucleophilic hydrolysis mechanism for PPP family phosphatases.
source: The structures thus provide direct evidence for the in-line nucleophilic hydrolysis mechanism for PPP family phosphatases, as outlined by the Barford and Ciszak groups (Egloff et al., 1995; Swingle et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with proposed mechanisms.

claim: The hydrophobic doublet L459-L460IRSp53/L1035-L1036spectrin (+4/+5) makes intimate contact with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket, entirely burying the +5 leucine sidechain.
source: In both structures, the residues +3 to +6 form a β-turn, allowing the hydrophobic doublet L459-L460IRSp53/L1035-L1036spectrin (+4/+5) to make intimate contact with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket, entirely burying the +5 leucine sidechain (Figure 4C and F).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claim: Alanine substitutions at positions S453 (−2), S454 (−1), and T456 (+1) in IRSp53 decreased catalytic efficiency somewhat, apparently reflecting an increased KM.
source: Alanine substitutions at positions S453 (−2), S454 (−1), and T456 (+1) decreased catalytic efficiency somewhat, apparently reflecting an increased KM.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claim: Alanine substitution of IRSp53 residues L459, L460, and D461 (+4 to +6) individually increased KM.
source: In contrast, alanine substitution of residues L459, L460, and D461 (+4 to +6) individually increased KM, but had variable effects on catalytic efficiency, with L459A and D461A increasing it, and L460A reducing it (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claim: The IRSp53 LL459/460AA mutant was essentially unreactive in the in vitro dephosphorylation assay.
source: Pairwise combination of substitutions at positions +4 through +6 suppressed reactivity even more, with the LL459/460AA mutant being essentially unreactive.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claim: IRSp53(L460A) exhibited enhanced basal phosphorylation and was less susceptible to CD-induced dephosphorylation than wildtype IRSp53 in NIH3T3 cells.
source: Upon expression in NIH3T3 cells, IRSp53(L460A) exhibited enhanced basal phosphorylation, and was less susceptible to CD-induced dephosphorylation than wildtype IRSp53, as assessed using the phospho-S455 antibody (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claim: Substrate interactions with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are important for efficient dephosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo.
source: These data show that substrate interactions with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are important for efficient dephosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data from both in vitro assays and cell-based experiments.

claim: Only peptides representing low KM substrates - IRSp53, spectrin αII, Tbc1d15 and Plekho2 - exhibited detectable binding in the peptide overlay assay.
source: Only peptides representing low KMsubstrates - IRSp53, spectrin αII, Tbc1d15 and Plekho2 - exhibited detectable binding under the conditions of the assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; see Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by peptide overlay assay data.

claim: Positions +4 and +5 in the substrate displayed the strongest selectivity in the peptide array, for hydrophobic residues and leucine respectively.
source: Analysis of both arrays implicated residues −2 to +7 in substrate-binding affinity. Positions +4 and +5 displayed the strongest selectivity, for hydrophobic residues and leucine respectively: indeed, phenylalanine substitution of IRSp53 L459 (+4), increased binding affinity and catalytic efficiency (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by peptide array data.

claim: Phenylalanine substitution of IRSp53 L459 (+4) increased binding affinity and catalytic efficiency.
source: Positions +4 and +5 displayed the strongest selectivity, for hydrophobic residues and leucine respectively: indeed, phenylalanine substitution of IRSp53 L459 (+4), increased binding affinity and catalytic efficiency (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by peptide array and phosphatase assay data.

claim: Interactions with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are a critical determinant of Phactr1/PP1 substrate recognition.
source: Taken together with the kinetics data, these results show that interactions with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are a critical determinant of Phactr1/PP1 substrate recognition.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including structural, kinetic, and binding data.

claim: In the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53(S455E) complex, IRSp53 T456 occupies the position corresponding to S455 in the wildtype complex.
source: Strikingly, in this complex, the phospomimetic glutamate (S455E) does not replace phosphate at the catalytic site. Instead, IRSp53 T456 occupies the position corresponding to S455 in the wildtype complex, with a recruited phosphate positioned as in the wild-type complex, and the glutamate (S455E) in effect occupies position −1, pointing away from the catalytic site (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53(S455E) complex.

claim: The critical contacts between IRSp53(S455E) L459/L460 and the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are maintained in the S455E complex.
source: Nevertheless, the critical contacts between IRSp53(S455E) L459/L460 and the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are maintained, extending the intervening sequence G457-N458-L459 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53(S455E) complex.

claim: Both wildtype IRSp53 pT456 and IRSp53 E455/pT456 were effective substrates for Phactr1/PP1, exhibiting three- to fivefold higher KM, but only twofold lower catalytic efficiency.
source: Consistent with this, both wildtype IRSp53 pT456 and IRSp53 E455/pT456 were effective substrates for Phactr1/PP1, exhibiting three- to fivefold higher KM, but only twofold lower catalytic efficiency, while IRSp53 pS453 and pS454 were very poor substrates, exhibiting 10–30 fold lower catalytic efficiency (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claim: IRSp53 pS453 and pS454 were very poor substrates for Phactr1/PP1, exhibiting 10–30 fold lower catalytic efficiency.
source: Consistent with this, both wildtype IRSp53 pT456 and IRSp53 E455/pT456 were effective substrates for Phactr1/PP1, exhibiting three- to fivefold higher KM, but only twofold lower catalytic efficiency, while IRSp53 pS453 and pS454 were very poor substrates, exhibiting 10–30 fold lower catalytic efficiency (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claim: Phactr1/PP1 substrates can tolerate either three or four residues between the target residue and the hydrophobic residue that engages the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket.
source: Thus, Phactr1/PP1 substrates can tolerate either three or four residues between the target residue and the hydrophobic residue that engages the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by structural and kinetic data from the S455E complex.

claim: Compared with apo-PP1 and spinophilin/PP1, Phactr1/PP1 exhibited 100- to 400-fold greater catalytic efficiency against its substrates IRSp53 pS455, CD2ap pS458, and afadin pS1275.
source: Compared with apo-PP1 and spinohilin/PP1, Phactr1/PP1 exhibited 100- to 400-fold greater catalytic efficiency against its substrates IRSp53 pS455, CD2ap pS458, and afadin pS1275 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by comparative phosphatase assay data.

claim: Phactr1/PP1 dephosphorylated cofilin pS3 with a low catalytic efficiency comparable to afadin pS1275, but this was only twofold enhanced compared with PP1 or spinophilin/PP1.
source: However, while Phactr1/PP1 dephosphorylated cofilin pS3 with a low catalytic efficiency comparable to afadin pS1275, this was only twofold enhanced compared with PP1 or spinophilin/PP1 (Figure 6E; see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by comparative phosphatase assay data.

claim: Phactr1 did not enhance the activity of PP1 against the GM/PP1 substrate glycogen phosphorylase pS15, or the spinophilin/PP1 target GluR1 pS863.
source: Phactr1 did not enhance the activity of PP1 against the GM/PP1 substrate glycogen phosphorylase pS15, or the spinophilin/PP1 target GluR1 pS863 (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by comparative phosphatase assay data.

claim: The PP1-Phactr1 fusion protein behaved similarly to the Phactr1/PP1 complex, indicating that RVxF interactions are not essential for specificity.
source: The PP1-Phactr1 fusion protein behaved similarly to the Phactr1/PP1 complex, indicating that RVxF interactions are not essential for specificity (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by comparative phosphatase assay data with the fusion protein.

claim: The composite surface formed by interaction with Phactr1 is responsible for the substrate specificity of the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme.
source: Taken together with the results in the preceding sections, these results show that the composite surface formed by interaction with Phactr1 is responsible for the substrate specificity of the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The sequence conservation between Phactr family members suggests that the other Phactr-family/PP1 holoenzymes will have similar specificity.
source: The sequence conservation between Phactr family members suggests that the other Phactr-family/PP1 holoenzymes will have similar specificity.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and inference.

claim: The overlap of the RVxF motif with RPEL3 explains why G-actin competes with PP1 to bind Phactr1 and Phactr4.
source: The overlap of the RVxF motif with RPEL3 explains why G-actin competes with PP1 to bind Phactr1 and Phactr4, allowing the formation of the Phactr1/PP1 complex to be controlled by fluctuations in actin dynamics (Huet et al., 2013; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and citations to previous work.

claim: Phactr1/PP1 dephosphorylates multiple target proteins involved in cytoskeletal structures or regulation.
source: We used proteomic approaches coupled with Phactr1 overexpression and inactivation studies to show that Phactr1/PP1 dephosphorylates multiple target proteins involved in cytoskeletal structures or regulation.
evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics data.

claim: IRSp53 was previously characterised as a Cdc42/Rac effector that controls F-actin assembly at membrane protrusions.
source: For example IRSp53 was previously characterised as a Cdc42/Rac effector that controls F-actin assembly at membrane protrusions (Scita et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scita et al., 2008.

claim: The Phactr1/PP1 target residue pS455 in IRSp53 is one of four negatively-acting putative AMPK sites that recruit 14-3-3 proteins.
source: The Phactr1/PP1 target residue pS455 characterised here is one of four negatively-acting putative AMPK sites that recruit 14-3-3 proteins (Cohen et al., 2011; Kast and Dominguez, 2019; Robens et al., 2010) and our data indicate another of these sites, S367, is also a Phactr1/PP1 target (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and phosphoproteomics data.

claim: IRSp53 S367 is also a Phactr1/PP1 target.
source: The Phactr1/PP1 target residue pS455 characterised here is one of four negatively-acting putative AMPK sites that recruit 14-3-3 proteins (Cohen et al., 2011; Kast and Dominguez, 2019; Robens et al., 2010) and our data indicate another of these sites, S367, is also a Phactr1/PP1 target (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics data.

claim: The Phactr1/PP1 sites in spectrin αII and girdin are adjacent to SH3 and SH2 domains, respectively.
source: Interestingly, the Phactr1/PP1 sites in spectrin αII and girdin are also adjacent to SH3 and SH2 domains, respectively (Lin et al., 2014; Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citation to Lin et al., 2014.

claim: Cofilin and destrin are dephosphorylated (and activated) by Phactr1.
source: Our data also confirm that the actin depolymerising factors cofilin and destrin are also dephosphorylated (and activated) by Phactr1, in agreement with previous studies of Phactr4 (Huet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics data and citation to Huet et al., 2013.

claim: Phactr1 is enriched at the post-synaptic density (PSD).
source: Phactr1 is enriched at the post-synaptic density (PSD) (Allen et al., 2004), and is required for neuronal migration and arborisation (Hamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Allen et al., 2004.

claim: Phactr1 is required for neuronal migration and arborisation.
source: Phactr1 is enriched at the post-synaptic density (PSD) (Allen et al., 2004), and is required for neuronal migration and arborisation (Hamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamada et al., 2018.

claim: Several Phactr1-dependent substrates in hippocampal neurons, including IRSp53 and spectrin αII, are dephosphorylated during long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: Several of these, including IRSp53 and spectrin αII, are dephosphorylated during long-term potentiation (LTP) (Li et al., 2016), and IRSp53-null mice exhibit deficits in hippocampal learning and memory (Bobsin and Kreienkamp, 2016; Kang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: IRSp53-null mice exhibit deficits in hippocampal learning and memory.
source: Several of these, including IRSp53 and spectrin αII, are dephosphorylated during long-term potentiation (LTP) (Li et al., 2016), and IRSp53-null mice exhibit deficits in hippocampal learning and memory (Bobsin and Kreienkamp, 2016; Kang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bobsin and Kreienkamp, 2016 and Kang et al., 2016.

claim: Dephosphorylation of cofilin is implicated in early-stage dendritic spine remodelling, along with G-actin itself.
source: Moreover, dephosphorylation of cofilin is implicated in early-stage dendritic spine remodelling, along with G-actin itself (Bosch et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bosch et al., 2014 and Lei et al., 2017.

claim: In humans, Phactr1 mutations cause the infantile seizure condition West syndrome.
source: These data suggest that rho-actin signalling to Phactr1 and the resulting protein dephosphorylations may contribute to synaptic plasticity, and indeed in humans Phactr1 mutations cause the infantile seizure condition West syndrome (Hamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamada et al., 2018.

claim: The inversion of the phosphate relative to its orientation in the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme provides support for the in-line nucleophilic attack model for PPP phosphatases.
source: The inversion of the phosphate relative to its orientation in the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme provides persuasive support for the in-line nucleophilic attack model for PPP phosphatases proposed by others (Egloff et al., 1995; Swingle et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with proposed mechanisms.

claim: Phactr1/PP1 substrates dock with the catalytic cleft in the opposite orientation to that previously seen in a complex between PP5 and a phosphomimetic substrate derivative.
source: We were surprised to see that Phactr1/PP1 substrates dock with the catalytic cleft in the opposite orientation to that previously seen in a complex between PP5 and a phosphomimetic substrate derivative (Oberoi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex.

claim: The additional binding energy provided by substrate interactions with the hydrophobic pocket is responsible for the enhanced catalytic rate of Phactr1/PP1 compared with apo-PP1 or other PP1 complexes.
source: Biochemical studies suggest that the additional binding energy provided by substrate interactions with the hydrophobic pocket is responsible for the enhanced catalytic rate of Phactr1/PP1 compared with apo-PP1 or other PP1 complexes.
evidence: This is based on biochemical data and inference.

claim: Substrates with higher KM might be more promiscuous in their interaction with PP1 complexes.
source: According to this view, it might be expected that substrates with higher KM might be more promiscuous in their interaction with PP1 complexes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the biochemical data.

claim: Cofilin pS3 might be a substrate that is more promiscuous in its interaction with PP1 complexes.
source: Cofilin pS3 might be such a substrate: it exhibits similar catalytic efficiency to afadin pS1275, but has little preference for Phactr1/PP1 over apo-PP1 or spinophilin/PP1.
evidence: This is based on biochemical data and speculation.

claim: High binding affinities might limit catalytic efficiency by slowing product dissociation.
source: However, high binding affinities might limit catalytic efficiency by slowing product dissociation, a situation perhaps exemplified by spectrin.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the biochemical data.

claim: Targeting the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface may be a good strategy to create specific Phactr/PP1 inhibitors.
source: PP1 inhibitors generally lack specificity because they target the catalytic site (Zhang et al., 2013), and our findings suggest that targeting the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface may be a good strategy to create specific Phactr/PP1 inhibitors.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural findings and citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Phactr/PP1 substrates can be defined by a hydrophobic doublet at position +4/+5 or +3/+4 relative to the dephosphorylation site, with leucine preferred at the distal position, embedded within acidic sequences.
source: We propose that Phactr/PP1 substrates can be defined by a hydrophobic doublet at position +4/+5 or +3/+4 relative to the dephosphorylation site, with leucine preferred at the distal position, embedded within acidic sequences.
evidence: This is a proposed consensus sequence based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: The simple Phactr1/PP1 core recognition sequence, S/T-x(2-3)-ϕ-L, is reminiscent of those seen for protein kinases.
source: The simple Phactr1/PP1 core recognition sequence, S/T-x(2-3)-ϕ-L, is reminiscent of those seen for protein kinases (Miller and Turk, 2018) and is perhaps the first identified for PP1.
evidence: This is based on comparison with kinase recognition sequences and citation to Miller and Turk, 2018.

claim: Mutation of positions +4 and/or +5 in candidate Phactr/PP1 substrates will be a useful way to generate authentic constitutively phosphorylated mutants for functional studies.
source: Mutation of positions +4 and/or +5 in candidate Phactr/PP1 substrates will be a useful way to generate authentic constitutively phosphorylated mutants for functional studies, as an alternative to 'phosphomimetic' glutamate substitution of the phosphorylated residue.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental strategy based on the findings.

claim: Spinophilin binds PP1 via a RVxF-ϕϕ-R-W string and remodels the PP1 hydrophobic groove differently than Phactr1.
source: In spinophilin, which also binds PP1 via a RVxF-ϕϕ-R-W string, sequences C-terminal to the W-motif form a helix that remodels the PP1 hydrophobic groove differently (Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with the spinophilin/PP1 complex and citation to Ragusa et al., 2010.

claim: Spinophilin does not detectably enhance PP1 activity towards Phactr/PP1 substrates.
source: Spinophilin therefore does not detectably enhance PP1 activity towards Phactr/PP1 substrates, although the relative contributions of the spinophilin-remodelled PP1 surface, and the adjacent PDZ domain, to substrate specificity remain to be determined (Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data and citation to Ragusa et al., 2010.

claim: MYPT interacts with PP1 in a different way to Phactr1 and spinophilin, extending both the C-terminal and acidic grooves.

claim: PIP-PP1 interaction acts indirectly to constrain substrate binding specificity by occluding potential substrate-binding sites on the PP1 surface such as the RVxF binding pocket.
source: In all these complexes, PIP-PP1 interaction also acts indirectly to constrain substrate binding specificity, by occluding potential substrate-binding sites on the PP1 surface such as the RVxF binding pocket (Ragusa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and citation to Ragusa et al., 2010.

claim: Phactr-family members do not appear to contain any conserved domains that might represent autonomous substrate-binding domains.
source: Phactr-family members do not appear to contain any conserved domains that might represent autonomous substrate-binding domains, as seen in NIPP1 (Boudrez et al., 2000) and PPP1R15A (Chen et al., 2015; Choy et al., 2015; Crespillo-Casado et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with other PIPs.

claim: Many PIPs act to target PP1 complexes to specific subcellular compartments, proteins or macromolecules.
source: On the other hand, many PIPs act to target PP1 complexes to specific subcellular compartments, proteins or macromolecules (Cohen, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cohen, 2002.

claim: Phactr-family proteins exhibit differential subcellular localisations, including the nucleus and cell membrane.
source: Phactr-family proteins exhibit differential subcellular localisations, including the nucleus and cell membrane (Huet et al., 2013; Wiezlak et al., 2012), and Phactr1 has been shown to interact directly with the KCNT1 potassium channel (Ali et al., 2020; Fleming et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huet et al., 2013 and Wiezlak et al., 2012.

claim: Phactr1 has been shown to interact directly with the KCNT1 potassium channel.
source: Phactr-family proteins exhibit differential subcellular localisations, including the nucleus and cell membrane (Huet et al., 2013; Wiezlak et al., 2012), and Phactr1 has been shown to interact directly with the KCNT1 potassium channel (Ali et al., 2020; Fleming et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ali et al., 2020 and Fleming et al., 2016.

claim: For Phactr3 and Phactr4, membrane targeting involves conserved N-terminal sequences.
source: At least for Phactr3 and Phactr4, membrane targeting involves conserved N-terminal sequences (Huet et al., 2013; Itoh et al., 2014) which overlap a G-actin controlled nuclear import signal in Phactr1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huet et al., 2013 and Itoh et al., 2014.

claim: The genetic dominance of West syndrome Phactr1 mutations and Phactr4 R536P/humdy mutation is consistent with Phactr-family proteins interacting with other cellular components in addition to PP1.
source: The genetic dominance of West syndrome Phactr1 mutations and Phactr4 R536P/humdy mutation also is consistent with Phactr-family proteins interacting with other cellular components in addition to PP1 (Hamada et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on genetic observations and citations to Hamada et al., 2018, Kim et al., 2007, and Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: The range of substrates controlled by Phactr1/PP1 in a particular setting will reflect the state of cellular actin dynamics and subcellular localisation of the complexes as well as the direct recognition of substrate primary sequence by the holoenzyme.
source: These considerations, and the coupling of Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme formation to rho-actin signalling, make it likely that the range of substrates controlled by Phactr1/PP1 in a particular setting will reflect the state of cellular actin dynamics and subcellular localisation of the complexes as well as the direct recognition of substrate primary sequence by the holoenzyme.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple considerations and inference.
